human_tolerance.notes: 'Due to its adaptability, the raccoon has been able to use urban areas as a habitat. The first sightings were recorded in a suburb of Cincinnati in the 1920s. Since the 1950s, raccoons have been present in metropolitan areas like Washington, D.C., Chicago, Toronto, and New York City.' Kassel has hosted Europe's densest urban population since the 1960s, about 50 to 150 animals per square kilometer; 'Fruit and insects in gardens and leftovers in municipal waste are easily available food sources', and 15-43% of urban raccoons sleep in abandoned or occupied houses.

phases.name: mating
phases.note: 'Raccoons usually mate in a period triggered by increasing daylight between late January and mid-March', with large regional differences: southern states mate later than average, and in Manitoba the mating season peaks later than usual in March and extends until June. Males roam their home ranges for the three- to four-day window when conception is possible.

phases.name: young
phases.note: Gestation 63 to 65 days (54 to 70 possible); a litter of typically two to five young is born, with the average varying from 2.5 in Alabama to 4.8 in North Dakota. Kits are born blind and deaf, 60-75 g and about 10 cm long, their mask already visible; ear canals open after about 18 to 23 days and the eyes a few days later; they explore outside the den at about 1 kg, take solid food at six to nine weeks and are usually weaned by 16 weeks.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: 'In the fall, after their mother has shown them dens and feeding grounds, the juvenile group splits up. While many females will stay close to the home range of their mother, males can sometimes move more than 20 km away. This is considered an instinctive behavior, preventing inbreeding.'

phases.name: dormancy
phases.note: 'In the northern parts of their range, raccoons go into a winter rest, reducing their activity drastically as long as a permanent snow cover makes searching for food difficult.' Colorado lies in the northern part of the range, so this phase is recorded for the locale; the fraction is judgement, since the source gives no proportion of the population that does it.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 41663 to 'Common Raccoon'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685). The Wikidata item sits at the title 'Raccoon', the current name of the English Wikipedia article; 'North American, northern or common raccoon' are listed there as synonyms.

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern. The Wikipedia article discusses population dynamics and introductions rather than listing a Red List category.

range.note: Native range from the Distribution sections ('Distribution in North America', 'Distribution outside North America', and the Germany and Japan sections) and introduced range from the former Soviet Union and Japan sections, which the source describes with named regions rather than a country list. US-CO is included as part of the North American distribution. The state list is an approximation of 'most of North America south of the Canadian Maritime provinces' and is not exhaustive. No elevation range is given in the source, so elevation_m is omitted.

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis) and locomotion modes: the source says raccoons 'depend on vertical structures to climb when they feel threatened', forage on the ground, and, in the northern part of the range, swim between lake and river shores whose amphibians and crustaceans are 'an important part of the raccoon's diet'. Individual numeric and behavioural traits below carry their own entries.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Tree hollows in old oaks or other trees and rock crevices are preferred by raccoons as sleeping, winter, and litter dens. If such dens are unavailable or accessing them is inconvenient, raccoons use burrows dug by other mammals, dense undergrowth, or tree crotches', plus hollows in old garden trees, cottages, garages, abandoned houses and attics in town. burrow is carried in habitat.resources as a secondary shelter rather than as the nest type.

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~8.5 kg); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Medium band.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the 'usually between 5 and 12 kg' band rather than of the full 2-26 kg range, because the source presents the narrower band as the typical case and notes mass 'varies considerably with habitat'.

traits.mass_range_kg.note: Stated range 2 to 26 kg. Males are usually 15 to 20% heavier than females, and a raccoon can weigh twice as much at the beginning of winter as in spring because of fat storage.

traits.length_m.note: The schema asks for nose to tail tip, and the source gives the two parts separately: head to hindquarters 40-70 cm (midpoint 55 cm) plus a bushy tail of 20-40 cm that 'is usually not much longer than 25 cm' (midpoint 30 cm). 85 cm is the sum of those two midpoints; using the tail's usual length rather than its maximum keeps the value typical.

traits.lifespan_y.note: 'the species' life expectancy in the wild is only 1.8 to 3.1 years, depending on the local conditions such as traffic volume, hunting, and weather severity'; midpoint 2.45 years. Captive raccoons are noted separately as living 'more than 20 years', which is not used.

traits.home_range_ha.note: Urban home ranges are 'only 3 to 40 hectares... for females and 8 to 80 hectares for males'; open-country prairie ranges are far larger (7 to 50 km2 for males in North Dakota). 40 ha is the midpoint of the urban male range and is the figure that fits the urban plot this record was written for; the much larger rural figure is recorded here rather than blended into it.

traits.diet.note: Directly sourced split: 'Its diet consists of about 40% invertebrates, 33% plant material and 27% vertebrates.' The plant third is divided between the items the source names - 'it prefers fruits and nuts, such as acorns and walnuts, which emerge in late summer and autumn' - and the occasional 'leaves and other vegetation'; the plant subdivision is judgement. The source also notes the diet is strongly seasonal, mostly insects, worms and other animals in spring and early summer, shifting to fruit and nuts in late summer and autumn.

traits.social.note: 'Related females often live in a so-called "fission-fusion society"... Unrelated males often form loose male social groups... Such a group does not usually consist of more than four individuals', and mothers isolate themselves with kits; Zeveloff 'concludes at least the females are solitary most of the time'. Solitary is the breeding and most-of-the-time structure; the group ceiling of four is the male-group figure.

traits.activity_pattern.note: 'Though usually nocturnal, the raccoon is sometimes active in daylight to take advantage of available food sources', with the winter-rest sentence in the Diet section confirming nocturnal foraging.

traits.defense.note: Judgement: the source describes climbing to vertical structures when threatened and descending steep trunks head-first as an escape, with no fight or mob behaviour, so Flee was authored.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement from the Urban raccoons section: the species has used urban areas as a habitat since the 1920s, sleeps in attics and garages, eats from gardens and municipal waste, and reaches 50-150 animals per square kilometre in Kassel, so a very low wariness value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Invertebrate, small_vertebrate, fruit, mast and water tags come from the Diet and Habitat sections; compost from 'leftovers in municipal waste'; cavity and burrow from the den hierarchy in the Habitat section. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: Habitat section: raccoons 'depend on vertical structures to climb when they feel threatened. Therefore, they avoid open terrain', sleep and den in tree hollows and rock crevices, and forage on the ground for the prey named in the Diet section, where insects, crayfish, fish, amphibians, bird eggs and shoreline animals dominate. The split is judgement but follows the source explicit statement that raccoons avoid open terrain alongside a ground-foraging diet.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Urban raccoons section, quoted at length in the field: first urban records in a Cincinnati suburb in the 1920s, metropolitan populations since the 1950s, Kassel's 50-150 animals per square kilometre since the 1960s, garden fruit and insects and municipal waste as food, and sleeping sites in garden-tree hollows, cottages, garages, abandoned houses and attics (15% of urban raccoons in Washington DC to 43% in Kassel).

seasonal.strategy.note: The source describes no migration and year-round activity, with a winter rest in the northern part of the range rather than true hibernation, so ActiveYearRound was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Daylight-triggered mating from late January to mid-March with the regional variations the source gives, gestation and litter sizes with the Alabama-to-North-D Dakota range, the kit development schedule, autumn dispersal with the 20 km male figure, and the northern winter rest. Day-of-month boundaries beyond the quoted late-January/mid-March are judgement. The winter-rest phase is tagged with a judgement fraction because the source says how many raccoons rest only as 'raccoons... go into a winter rest', not as a proportion.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Reproduction section: kits 'are blind and deaf at birth, but their mask is already visible against their light fur', 60-75 g and roughly 10 cm long; ear canals open at about 18-23 days, eyes a few days later; solid food at six to nine weeks; weaned by 16 weeks; the juvenile group splits up in autumn. duration_days 210 is derived from weaning at about 16 weeks to the mid-September-to-November dispersal window, and scale 0.45 is judgement for a newly weaned animal; requires_tag records that a den must be present.

vocalizations.note: HONEST GAP: the record carries an empty vocalizations list, which the schema permits for silent species, because the Raccoon article contains no description, transcription or naming of any raccoon call - the words 'vocalis', 'chitter', 'growl', 'scream' and 'purr' do not appear in it. Raccoons certainly vocalise; no openly-licensed description was found, so none was invented. This also means the behaviour program is used without a call slot, which fsm-ground-forager-v1 does not declare.

look.note: Physical characteristics section: 'The most characteristic physical feature of the raccoon is the area of black fur around the eyes, which contrasts sharply with the surrounding white face coloring... reminiscent of a "bandit's mask"', 'the slightly rounded ears are also bordered by white fur', 'the long and stiff guard hairs, which shed moisture, are usually colored in shades of gray and to a lesser extent brown', with 'the alternating light and dark rings on the tail'. The mask is drawn by colouring the head slot with the near-black marking colour and the muzzle and ear rims with the pale belly colour; the ringed tail is approximated by the dark tail colour. Proportions are authored judgement, set from the 40-70 cm head-to-hindquarters length and the 23-30 cm shoulder height.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared ground-forager program: food_tag is the 40% invertebrate share, the largest single component of a diet the program can express as one tag; flee_m and calm_m are judgement for an animal that flees to the nearest climbable structure but has a small home range in town; flee_gait and forage_gait are both walk, since the source describes ambling ground foraging and climbing rather than a run; the rest window 8-88 degrees of sun elevation puts rest in the middle of the day, matching a nocturnal species that 'is sometimes active in daylight to take advantage of available food sources'.
